I used to take my dog for several walks a day and he was still wild. We started taking him to an active doggy daycare two days a week and that has completely changed his disposition and saved our sanity. It costs us close to 50 dollars a week but the behavior change has been priceless.

My partner and I both work full time, 8-5pm every day. Here is some of my advice:

1. Find a breed that fits the energy level you can handle. If you get a high-energy dog, be prepared to take them to a dog park for a few hours every day.

2. Consider crate training early on; just because you can't handle the idea of being confined in a crate all day doesn't mean a dog feels the same way. It's a fantastic way to potty train a dog, and many dogs like their kennels as it provides them security and solitude.

3. Consider doggy daycare a few days a week. We have our dog go to daycare on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and he comes home completely exhausted and happy. This costs around 50 dollars a week, and we alternate dropping him off and picking him up.

4. 30 minutes over lunch is fine; you're right, puppies can't hold their bladder. You will need to go home to let him out.

5. It sounds like you have a yard; I'd invest in an invisible fence at least. It's very nice to just let the dog out when it needs to go or to hang out in the yard and let the dog play.

Good luck!

Edit: One more thing, start off more strict and get more lax as time goes on. Sure, you might want a puppy in your bed, but do you want a full-grown dog sleeping with you every night? I'm of the opinion that you should start teaching behaviors that you want early, then start giving them more slack as they get older and you find what you want your dog to actually do. For instance, our dog didn't go in our bed for the first 3 months; now that he is fully crate trained, we let him sleep in with us every now and again on the weekend. It's much harder to train behavior down the road, just my two cents.

I'm a 34-year-old man and I don't want children. This topic comes up within the first month of dating someone. It's a pretty big deal breaker and you should have talked about this a long time ago. Since that ship has sailed, feel free to open the discussion by asking him what he thinks about kids and then bringing in your opinion during that conversation.

What's wrong with you? Who knows. There is something wrong with each and every one of us in various ways. I wouldn't focus on you being inherently broken. If anything, you should realize that you at least have the insight to understand that you're kind of messed up in some way or another.

One problem I do notice though, you do seem to live a lot in your head. You are telling us things, very important things, that you haven't brought up to your partner at all (and you've been dating for 1.5 years!!). You need to be more upfront with what you're looking for in a relationship and what some of your deal breakers are.

Just a few tips:

1. Your relationship should not be the only thing that fulfills you in your life. You can't look at one person to provide your sole sense of purpose and happiness (whether that is through activities, shared interests, whatever).

2. Talk about these 'deal breaker' type issues early on in a relationship. You shouldn't be wondering if he wants kids when you don't after a year and a half. That is not good.

3. Stop worrying about how messed up you are. It's unhealthy and skews your perspective on life. You've already been through therapy and seem to have made a lot of progress. Were you honest with your therapist about all your feelings? Maybe it is time to go back again.

4. You're a strong and independent woman (obviously). Don't be afraid to be by yourself and wait for exactly what you want to come to you. Don't feel like you need a relationship to define your existence. When you're happy by yourself, then you're ready for a relationship.

Besides all of that, maybe you should try to date a different type of guy if all your exes seem to be in similar fields or just similar types of guys in general. I'm dating someone who is different from anyone else I've ever dated and I found it's exactly what I've been missing. She is quirky and doesn't take life too seriously...I've always dated somewhat serious women who wanted family and I found out that simply isn't what I wanted.

Most of the gaming enthusiasts aren't addicted to single-player experiences; it tends to be the shooters, the massively multiplayer online games, the multiplayer online battle arena type of games. What is unique about these is

1. People rely on you, and you feel a bond and a need to play and keep them happy.
2. The content rarely changes; you're doing the same thing over and over again.
3. It's addictive and provides you with 'rewards' to keep playing and engaging.

I'd argue that books at least increase your vocabulary and expand your views on the world. Depending on the type of television you're watching, you may be learning from documentaries, etc. Gaming is just purely for enjoyment and really has no benefit at all, other than the enjoyment you get from playing (which should not be negated).

I still game...hell, I took a weekend off to play a tactical strategy game and I loved it. After I was done though, I couldn't help a nagging feeling that I really accomplished nothing and it was wasted time (other than what I enjoyed from leisure).

I suppose, like everything else in life...balance.

1. Did you take care of your body when you were younger? Did you participate in high-impact sports? You're probably already living with nagging injuries.

2. What is your body type? Do you have a very thin frame with slender wrists and ankles? You might find that it's a bit harder to gain the mass you want. Lifting heavy or very heavy weights is going to be a struggle with your tendons picking up the slack.

3. Warmups become more important than ever, especially in the shoulder region. I'm in my mid-thirties and always warm up on the treadmill for 5-10 minutes and do some fairly intensive shoulder warm-ups.

4. Never start heavy; always build up to heavy with warm-up sets.

5. If you're trying a new workout or routine, be careful and ease your way into it.

Being in your mid-thirties to early forties isn't old, but you're definitely at a higher risk for injury.

37m with 34f partner, child free and committed to being child free forever.

I never liked kids very much. I see a lot of people posting here about having nieces and nephews that they love and spoil...but I find kids generally annoying and not fun to be around.

That being said, I do tend to shower my nephew with gifts.

I suppose I'll start with the negatives

- Life can seem less purposeful. People that have children often derive all their life's purpose from raising and providing for them. This gives you a reason to do things day to day, that you may not want to do. Human beings are very purpose-driven creatures. Many also find fulfillment in spirituality. I don't want kids and I don't believe in a higher power, so purpose can be a struggle.

- No one will be there to look after you when you're older. That being said, a lot of kids aren't that great of caretakers anyway and you'll just as often find yourself in a bad situation with them, as without.

- No carrying on your family line. To me, I don't care. To many, they do want to carry on their family. This is something I never really understood. As someone without much of an ego, it always struck me that we're unusually attached to our individual family units and really don't care much about society as a whole.

- It becomes harder to make new friends as you get older. Old friends have kids and they are focusing on their family (as they should), but it can be very hard to make new friendships with child-free people of similar tastes.

- People that have children tend to go out far less and are far more available to work more. As someone who often has weekend plans or evening plans, I've noticed there is quite the culture of people with kids to be constantly home and constantly available to work. It can be frustrating. You'd think that having kids gives you less time...which it does, but your available time is often you being at home.

Onto the positives

- We travel a lot. In the past two years, I've been to various countries and cities that most people with children probably never get to see. These experiences have been great, looking forward to more.

- Freedom to do whatever you want to do. This weekend, we watched a popular fantasy film series, hung out with some friends, have a weekly tradition of watching sports at a local venue, and we went for a romantic winter walk.

- Pets can really fill a part of the void of children. We have two dogs and they give us both a lot of joy.

- More time for actually helping the world. Rather than focusing on your offspring, I can volunteer with organizations that I care about and actually make the world better as a whole, instead of just focusing on raising another human being who is going to just consume. I'm making much more of a difference in the world than most parents end up making.

- Retire early (hopefully)

I don't regret it at all. That being said, I do have a friend that I like a lot who has two kids, a great partner, great kids, great jobs and they seem truly blissful and happy. When I see them, I want to want to have children, but the urge just isn't in me.

All that being said, you aren't guaranteed a healthy child. You aren't guaranteed a smart child. You aren't guaranteed a child that will not get addicted to substances. You aren't guaranteed a child that will call or visit when you're older. You're not guaranteed anything.

If you're not ready to have a child under difficult circumstances, you're probably not ready to ever have kids.
